deep.reconstruction:
This page is very faint. It is largely bleed-through and the reverse of a sheet in the 'PH.Dioptrik' bundle. Only the heading block and the general layout can be read with any confidence. Everything below that goes beyond the visible fragments is my interpretation and is marked as such.

(1) Heading text. The fragments read roughly: '... [ge]brochen werden soll, ... auf folgende Art berechnet: 1) Jeder Punkt einer Geraden ... Richtung ...; 2) Jeder Punkt auf ... [Höhe/Ebene] ... in der Ebene ... y = 3 + 2x ... gerechnet wird.' This is a setup for tracing a ray (a straight line in the meridional plane) through an optical system. The ray is described as a line in coordinates (x along the axis, y the height above the axis). An example line y = 3 + 2x appears to be used as an illustration of how a line is specified.

(2) Next line, partly legible: 'x = f cot ..., c = ... / ... = ... / ...'. My interpretation: the intercept c of the ray with the axis is expressed through a height and an inclination, i.e. c = x − y·cot λ, or in the equivalent quotient form c = (...)/(...).

(3) Next line: 'λ Neigung des Strahles gegen die Axe' followed by the formula y = f tan λ = (x − c) tan λ. This is legible in outline. So λ is the inclination of the ray to the optical axis, and the ray meets the axis at x = c. The height of the ray at abscissa x is therefore y = (x − c)·tan λ. Where the distance from the axis crossing is called f, this is y = f·tan λ. This is the elementary parametrisation of a meridional ray.

(4) Numerical work. Below the heading are three columns of 7-decimal logarithmic computation. Probable readings:
- Left column: log values 9.7754563, 9.0533172, 9.2526..., 9.44..., an angle-like value 89.61252 (or 89°...) with a remark, and further logs 8.3284..., 8.4..., 9.6523..., 9.66....
- Middle column: logs 9.7665682, 9.6..., then 102.8115... and 41.945, a small quantity 0.0348..., two struck-out lines, and further logs 8.6498..., 9.11..., 9.2279..., 9.7525..., 8.6..., 9.79....
- Right column: illegible.

The pattern of logs of sines/tangents (characteristics 8 and 9), angles, and distances is what one expects from successive application of the refraction law (sin i' = sin i / n) at spherical surfaces. Such a computation finds intercepts and inclinations of a ray after each surface; this interpretation is mine.

Context: the next page records measured separations, diameters and focal lengths of the lenses A, m, B, C, n, D, E of a telescope or eyepiece system, in mm and Paris lines. This page is presumably a trigonometric ray trace through such a system. The individual numerical steps cannot be reconstructed or checked from the image.

results.what: Description of a meridional ray by its axis intercept c and inclination λ: y = (x − c) tan λ, with c obtained from a point on the ray and its slope.
results.modern_name: Paraxial/meridional ray parametrisation (intercept–slope form) used in trigonometric ray tracing
results.usually_credited_to: Standard optics practice (18th–19th century; e.g. Euler, Klügel, later Seidel)

results.what: Logarithmic numerical trace of a ray through a lens system (probable interpretation of the columns of 7-figure logs).
results.modern_name: Trigonometric (exact) ray tracing through spherical surfaces
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice; Gauss's Dioptrische Untersuchungen (1841) is his published dioptrics work

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a faint working sheet of routine ray-trace arithmetic in Gauss's dioptrics context. His interest in such computations is well known, and nothing non-standard is legible.

checkable.asserts: With c = x0 − y0·cot λ, the line through (x0, y0) with inclination λ is y = (x − c) tan λ; the expression should simplify to 0.
The example line y = 3 + 2x meets the axis at c = −3/2, with tan λ = 2.
